messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: feedback on hierarchical model tutorial
parts:
Before releasing to our users, I'd like to get some feedback
on a knitr doc I wrote as an intro to hierarchical modeling
for repeated binary trials. It lives here:

stan-dev/example-models/knitr/efron-morris/pool-no-pool.Rmd

As usual, I had a hard time judging what to explain and what
to take for granted. I tried to focus on Stan. Any tips on
making the RStan better would be appreciated. Andrew, now's the
time to jump in on ggplot2 defaults! Or I can ask you in person
and we can create a theme you can live with.

I'm happy to send the 2.8MB HTML file it produced (encapsulated)
if you'd rather not run it yourself. (If you do want to run it,
you only need:

> rmarkdown::render("pool-no-pool.Rmd")

to get the basic HTML. I couldn't get it to keep the figures
separate, even trying what Ben suggested (I'm probably doing it
wrong).

Here's the abstract:

This note illustrates the effects on posterior inference of pooling
data (aka sharing strength) across items for repeated binary trial
data. It provides Stan models and R code to fit and check predictive
models for three situations: (a) complete pooling, which assumes each
item is the same, (b) no pooling, which assumes the items are
unrelated, and (c) partial pooling, where the similarity among the
items is estimated. We consider two hierarchical models to estimate
the partial pooling, one with a beta prior on chance of success and
another with a normal prior on the log odds of success. The note
explains with working examples how to (i) fit models in RStan and plot
the results in R ussing ggplot2, (ii) estimate event probabilities,
(iii) evaluate posterior predictive densities to compare model
predictions, (iv) rank items by chance of success, (v) perform
multiple comparisons in several settings, (vi) replicate new data for
posterior p-values, and (vii) perform graphical posterior predictive
checks.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] feedback on hierarchical model tutorial
parts:
Section: Repeated Binary Trials

I would reference n \in N in the opening sentence, otherwise the n subscripts don’t make sense until the next few sentences have been read.

“any ML conference proceedings” or “all ML conference proceedings”? :-p

Emphasize that you are using the remaining data to determine _predictive performance_.

Put “The data separates the outcome from the initial 45 at-bats from the rest of the season.” after the display of the data. Perhaps something like “The data are separated into the first 45 at bats of the season and the remaining at bats; we will use the first 45 at bats to build our model and then the remaining at bats to test the predictive performance of our model.”

Section: Pooling

There’s an awkward line break after the first two sentences.

You haven’t defined a population distribution yet so the the discussion of variances has no context here. If you wanted to include this note here, I would introduce another sentence like “Partial pooling is typically accomplished with a hierarchical or population model, where the individuals assumed to have been are drawn from a population normally distributed with mean mu and variance sigma2. When the population variance is infinite partial pooling is equivalent to no pooling, while zero population variance is equivalent to complete pooling”. Or just leave this discussion to the partial pooling section (although you don’t use a normal hierarchical model there, so the relevant of this point is questionable).

Section: Model 1: Complete Pooling

Do you want () or [] here? Typically 0 and 1 are considered valid values, in which case you want [0, 1].

“The consequences for leaving the constraint off is that the program may fail during random initialization or during an iteration because it will try values…” What is “it”? Maybe something like “…because Stan will consider mathematically invalid values outside of (0, 1)”.

The proportion sign hasn’t been used yet, why is it being described here?

“The model can be fit as follows, reading…” -> “The model can be fit as follows: <fit input>”. Note that the data are read out of the R environment by name…”

Section: Model 3: Partial Pooling (Chance of Success)

I recommend running with the default step size and adapt_delta and discuss the errors that show up. Mention how the errors indicate that Stan isn’t fitting well and we can try to tweak the step size and adapt_delta to improve the fit. It helps, but the mixing is still bad so we need a better solution (which then motivates the next section).

The Beta distribution isn’t a location-scale distribution so it is not immediately amenable to the centering/non-centering discussion. But it can be manipulated into a location-scale family by unconstraining its parameters, in which case you center/non-center the unconstrained parameters. Essentially you’ll end up with something like the model in the next section anyways.

Section: Model 4: Partial Pooling (Log Odds)

Yup, the distribution for mu and sigma will still look like a weak funnel (when the random effect variation is large, there is a weak non-identifiability between the mean and the average of the random effects). What you want to be looking at is the distribution of the random effects, alpha, verses sigma. That’s what causes all of the problems in the fit.

Section: Observed vs. Estimated Chance of Success

It would be great if more of the plot could be labeled to avoid having to describe everything in the text.

Section: Posterior Predictive Distribution

You never discuss what you can do with the predictive distribution, let alone why they provide a ranking that might approximate relative performance. This leaves a big gap when you move on to the explicit calculations.

Section: Posterior p-Values

I highly recommend a comment here about how posterior predictive p-values can’t really be calibrated (no power calculations can be done because there is no alternative hypothesis). This means that we can’t formally distinguish between a bad fit or unlikely data, and we have to be careful in how we interpret these values. Ultimately what we do in practice is assume that for small enough p-values there has to be some alternative model that fits better, and if we see such small p-values we start looking for that alternate model by expanding our null model.

you're suggesting here.

> Section: Posterior p-Values
>
> I highly recommend a comment here about how posterior predictive p-values can’t really be calibrated (no power calculations can be done because there is no alternative hypothesis). This means that we can’t formally distinguish between a bad fit or unlikely data, and we have to be careful in how we interpret these values. Ultimately what we do in practice is assume that for small enough p-values there has to be some alternative model that fits better, and if we see such small p-values we start looking for that alternate model by expanding our null model.

Not at all sure what this means and I'm uncomfortable dropping in
a paragraph I don't understand.

Isn't it always the case for hypothesis tests that we can't distinguish
bad model vs. unlikely data? That is, we'll falsely reject null hypotheses
when we are faced with unlikely data.

- Bob

So we have the sections:

Posterior Predictive Distribution
- Define the posterior predictive distribution
Evaluating Held-Out Data Predictions
- This is just a definition, there’s no motivation for what held-out data predictions can be used.
Simulating Replicated Data
- For what is this replicated data useful? Ultimately to compute posterior predictive expectations
but that’s not made clear here.
Prediction for New Trials
- Here’s where you make the jump. You talk about evaluating models, but you just assume that
held-out predictive likelihood is the right measure without any discussion as to why.

>> Section: Posterior p-Values
>>
>> I highly recommend a comment here about how posterior predictive p-values can’t really be calibrated (no power calculations can be done because there is no alternative hypothesis). This means that we can’t formally distinguish between a bad fit or unlikely data, and we have to be careful in how we interpret these values. Ultimately what we do in practice is assume that for small enough p-values there has to be some alternative model that fits better, and if we see such small p-values we start looking for that alternate model by expanding our null model.
>

> a paragraph I don't understand.
>
> Isn't it always the case for hypothesis tests that we can't distinguish
> bad model vs. unlikely data? That is, we'll falsely reject null hypotheses
> when we are faced with unlikely data.

It is if you don’t compute a power! That’s part of the reason why significance
tests are somewhat meaningless without a power calculation. In the predictive
validation case we don’t have an alternative hypothesis so we can’t compute
anything like a power, and we’re left with the fundamental ambiguity.

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] feedback on hierarchical model tutorial
parts:
Bob, this is awesome. I finally had a chance to read through most of it.
I think the others have made good recommendations already, but I do have one
suggestion about the R code, which is that the with() function is very useful.
There are several places where it can make your code simpler:

1) You have:

df <- data.frame(FirstName = df$FirstName,
LastName = df$LastName,
Hits = df$Hits,
At.Bats = df$At.Bats,
RemainingAt.Bats = df$RemainingAt.Bats,
RemainingHits = df$SeasonHits - df$Hits)

but you can do the same thing like this:

df <- with(df, data.frame(FirstName, LastName,
Hits, At.Bats,
RemainingAt.Bats,
RemainingHits = SeasonHits - Hits))

which avoids the df$ on every line and the repetition of variable names (which are both pet peeves of mine, but maybe that's just me).

2) The same thing goes for working with the lists that rstan::extract returns. For
example, this

phi_sim <- ss_hier$phi;
kappa_sim <- ss_hier$kappa;
df_bda3_fig_5_3 <- data.frame(x = log(phi_sim / (1 - phi_sim)),
y = log(kappa_sim));

can be done in one line without the intermediate steps of creating phi_sim and
kappa_sim:

df_bda3_fig_5_3 <- with(ss_hier, data.frame(x = log(phi / (1 - phi)),
y = log(kappa)))

3) You can do the same thing later in the file when working with the next model:

mu_sim <- ss_hier_logit$mu;
sigma_sim <- ss_hier_logit$sigma;
df_bda3_fig_5_3_logit <- data.frame(x = mu_sim,
y = log(sigma_sim));

can all be replaced with the one line

df_bda3_fig_5_3_logit <- with(ss_hier_logit, data.frame(x = mu_sim,
y = log(sigma_sim)))


Again, this really is a fantastic tutorial. And of course feel free to ignore my R code preferences. The way you have it now definitely works just fine.

I think the approach is generalizable in the way you tried, but the error just comes from the fact that you don't actually have an "alpha" in ss_hier_logit, but rather only alpha_std (it doesn't look like alpha gets created in the Stan program). So that's why your first way doesn't work. You'd think that the second way would also fail then, but using "$" allows for partial name matching so it's accessing ss_hier_logit$alpha_std when you use ss_hier_logit$alpha. This is often convenient for interactive programming but it drives me nuts that it's the default (one of the many things about R that drives me nuts).

Jonah

> Here's the abstract:

> This note illustrates the effects on posterior inference of pooling
> data (aka sharing strength) across items for repeated binary trial
> data. It provides Stan models and R code to fit and check predictive
> models for three situations: (a) complete pooling, which assumes each
> item is the same, (b) no pooling, which assumes the items are
> unrelated, and (c) partial pooling, where the similarity among the
> items is estimated. We consider two hierarchical models to estimate
> the partial pooling, one with a beta prior on chance of success and
> another with a normal prior on the log odds of success. The note
> explains with working examples how to (i) fit models in RStan and plot
> the results in R ussing ggplot2, (ii) estimate event probabilities,
> (iii) evaluate posterior predictive densities to compare model
> predictions, (iv) rank items by chance of success, (v) perform
> multiple comparisons in several settings, (vi) replicate new data for
> posterior p-values, and (vii) perform graphical posterior predictive
> checks.
